category.name: Transport & Tracking
category.description: Aircraft and vessel movement, registration and ownership. Aviation and maritime are unusually transparent domains because both broadcast position by design and both maintain public registries, which makes them among the most productive areas in open-source investigation.

tools.name: Flightradar24
tools.summary: The most widely used live flight tracker, combining a crowdsourced ADS-B receiver network with other data sources.
tools.description:
Flightradar24 aggregates ADS-B position broadcasts from a large volunteer receiver network, supplemented by satellite-based ADS-B, MLAT for older transponders and scheduled-flight data. It shows live positions and, on paid tiers, historical playback going back years.

Investigators use it for two things: establishing that a specific aircraft was at a specific place at a specific time, and identifying an aircraft seen or photographed. Registration lookups tie a tail number to type, operator and route history, which is the entry point to ownership research.

The blind spots are systematic and must be understood before drawing conclusions. Coverage depends on receivers being within range, so it is excellent over Europe and North America and patchy over oceans, deserts and much of Africa and Central Asia. Aircraft can and do switch off ADS-B. Military and many state aircraft are filtered or blocked, and there are opt-out schemes that remove private aircraft from public display. A gap in a track is not evidence an aircraft was not there — it is usually evidence of no receiver.
tools.costNotes: Free live tracking with limited history and filtering. Paid subscription tiers extend historical playback, add filters, alerts and export, and a separate commercial data offering exists. Current prices were not verified in this review.
tools.legalNotes: ADS-B is an unencrypted broadcast intended to be received, and receiving it is lawful in most jurisdictions — though a small number restrict reception or publication of aircraft movements, so check locally. Terms of service restrict scraping and redistribution of the platform's data. Tracking a specific individual's private aircraft to infer their movements is processing personal data about that person and needs a genuine journalistic or investigative justification; several such projects have drawn legal threats.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Position data is derived from the aircraft's own broadcast and is accurate where received. Coverage gaps are the dominant limitation and are invisible in the interface, which is how analysts wrongly conclude an aircraft 'disappeared'. Some displayed information — operator, aircraft type, and estimated positions across gaps — is inferred or sourced from databases that contain errors. Corroborate any critical movement claim against a second tracking source.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established market-leading service. Not fetched during this review; subscription tiers and history depth change periodically.

tools.name: ADS-B Exchange
tools.summary: Unfiltered ADS-B aggregator that historically displayed aircraft other trackers suppress.
tools.description:
ADS-B Exchange built its reputation on a single editorial decision: it did not honour the blocking and filtering schemes that remove military, government and opted-out private aircraft from other trackers. That made it the source of record for a great deal of open-source reporting on state aircraft, surveillance flights and the movements of private jets belonging to public figures.

It was acquired by JETNET, an aviation data company, in a deal announced in January 2023 and reported at around $20 million. The acquisition was contentious in the volunteer feeder community precisely because the platform's value rested on a community commitment to non-filtering under community control.

Anyone relying on it should verify its current filtering policy and data-access terms directly rather than assuming the pre-acquisition position still holds. Its distinguishing feature is a policy, and policies change with ownership.
tools.costNotes: The map has historically been free to view. API and historical data access have been sold, with contributors who feed data traditionally receiving access benefits. The current pricing and access model following the JETNET acquisition was not verified in this review and should be confirmed before it is relied on.
tools.legalNotes: Receiving ADS-B broadcasts is lawful in most jurisdictions. Displaying aircraft that opt-out schemes ask to be suppressed is lawful but has repeatedly drawn political and legal pressure, and reporting on an identified individual's private flights is a personal-data processing act needing a genuine public-interest basis. Check the current terms on redistribution before republishing bulk data.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Where its receiver network covers, the data is the aircraft's own broadcast and is accurate. The same coverage-gap caveat as any ADS-B network applies. The material uncertainty here is not technical but editorial — whether the unfiltered policy that made it distinctive remains fully in force under the current owner. Verify before citing it as an unfiltered source.
tools.confidenceNotes: The JETNET acquisition, announced January 2023 and reported at approximately $20 million, was confirmed during this review. The current filtering policy, free-access terms and API pricing were explicitly not verified and should be checked before relying on this entry's historical characterisation.

tools.name: The OpenSky Network
tools.summary: Non-profit research ADS-B network with a large open historical archive and API access for academic use.
tools.description:
OpenSky is a community-operated, research-oriented ADS-B receiver network run as a non-profit with academic roots. Its distinguishing asset is the historical archive: it retains raw and processed position data going back years and makes it available for research through an API and bulk datasets.

That makes it the right choice when the question is analytical rather than observational — reconstructing a flight pattern over months, studying a fleet's behaviour, or producing reproducible results that another researcher can independently check. Commercial trackers gate history behind subscriptions and their terms rarely permit that kind of reuse.

Access is tiered by purpose. Academic and non-commercial research use is generously provisioned, and contributing a receiver improves your access. Commercial use is treated differently and requires arrangement. Coverage follows the volunteer network and is uneven, with the same gap caveats as any ADS-B source.
tools.costNotes: Free for research and non-commercial use with a registered account, with better allowances for users who feed data to the network. Commercial use requires separate arrangement. Specific current rate limits were not verified in this review — the site returned HTTP 403 to automated fetching, which is routine bot filtering rather than an availability problem.
tools.legalNotes: Non-commercial research terms are explicit and must be honoured — using research-tier access for commercial work breaches them. As with all flight data, tracking an identified individual's movements is personal-data processing requiring justification. Publishing derived datasets requires attention to the network's data-sharing conditions.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Data is raw and well documented, which is exactly what makes it good for research and demanding for casual use — you get closer to the sensor and further from a polished interface. Coverage is thinner than the large commercial networks, with substantial gaps outside Europe and North America. The long archive is its decisive advantage and is well suited to reproducible analysis.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established academic network. The site returned HTTP 403 to automated fetching during this review, consistent with bot filtering rather than any change in status, so this is marked high rather than verified.

tools.name: FlightAware
tools.summary: Flight tracking with strong North American coverage and access to filed flight plans and operator data.
tools.description:
FlightAware combines its own ADS-B receiver network with air traffic control data feeds, which gives it an advantage in the United States: it can show filed flight plans, scheduled and actual departure and arrival times, and routing information that pure ADS-B reception does not provide.

For investigations concerning general and business aviation in North America this is often the better source, and its per-tail history is useful for establishing an aircraft's pattern of operation — which airports it frequents, which operator files for it, how often it flies.

Coverage and depth fall off outside North America, and the most useful historical and export capabilities sit behind paid tiers. It also honours the US aircraft-blocking programmes, so private aircraft whose owners have requested suppression will not appear.
tools.costNotes: Free tracking with limited history and advertising, plus paid subscription tiers for extended history, alerts and export, and a separate commercial data API sold by volume. Current prices were not verified in this review.
tools.legalNotes: Honours US aircraft-owner blocking programmes, so its data is not unfiltered and should not be described as such. Terms of service restrict scraping and redistribution. Reporting on the movements of an identified individual's aircraft carries the usual personal-data justification requirement.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Strong and well-corroborated in North America where it has ATC-derived data in addition to ADS-B. Weaker elsewhere. Filed flight plans state intent, not outcome — an aircraft that filed for a destination did not necessarily go there, and treating a filed plan as a movement record is a common error. Blocked aircraft are silently absent.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established commercial service. Not fetched during this review; tier structure and pricing change periodically.

tools.name: Planespotters.net
tools.summary: Community database of aircraft registrations, fleet histories and photographs, with dated ownership changes.
tools.description:
Planespotters.net maintains detailed per-airframe records assembled by aviation enthusiasts: construction number, type, registration history, every operator the airframe has flown for with dates, current status, and a large archive of dated photographs.

The registration and operator history is the investigative payload. Aircraft change registration and operator frequently, often as a deliberate way of obscuring ownership, and a chain of registrations across leasing companies and jurisdictions is exactly what you need to trace to identify a beneficial owner. The photographs are independently useful: a dated photograph of a specific airframe places it at an airport on a date, and photographs often capture livery changes that mark ownership transitions.

Limits: it is enthusiast-maintained, so accuracy is generally high but unverified, and coverage of commercial fleets is far better than of small private aircraft. Records lag real changes. Corroborate against the relevant national aircraft registry.
tools.costNotes: Free to browse without an account, supported by advertising. Some contributor features require registration.
tools.legalNotes: Aggregated public aviation data and contributor photographs. Photographs are the photographers' copyright and are not free to republish without permission — this is a routinely violated condition. Aircraft ownership data may indirectly identify individuals.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Enthusiast communities are unusually rigorous about airframe data and the records are generally accurate and well cross-checked, but nothing here is authoritative and there is no formal verification process. Registry changes appear with a lag. Use it to build the ownership chain, then confirm each link against the national registry of the relevant jurisdiction.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established community database. Not fetched during this review.

tools.name: FAA Aircraft Registry Inquiry
tools.summary: The official US civil aircraft register — authoritative N-number lookup with registered owner details.
tools.description:
The Federal Aviation Administration's registry is the authoritative record for US-registered aircraft. Searching by N-number, serial number or registered-owner name returns the aircraft type, serial, airworthiness classification, and the registered owner's name and address, along with registration dates.

This is the primary source that community databases derive from, and it is what you cite. It is also downloadable in bulk, which makes owner-name searches across the whole register possible — a productive technique for finding aircraft associated with a company or trust.

The critical limitation for investigation is structural rather than technical: a very large share of US aircraft are registered to owner trusts and single-purpose LLCs whose sole function is to hold the aircraft and obscure the beneficial owner. The registry gives you the trustee, not the person. Getting past that requires corporate research, which is where this category hands off to Corporate & Financial.
tools.costNotes: Free, no account, with bulk downloadable registry files published.
tools.legalNotes: US federal public record, lawful to search and cite. Registered-owner records include names and addresses of natural persons where an aircraft is individually owned — publishing a private individual's home address obtained this way is a separate editorial and ethical decision from using it as a research lead.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Authoritative for US registration as filed. Two caveats: registered owner is frequently a trust or shell with no relation to actual control, and registry records reflect filings that may be stale between a sale and its recording. It tells you what the register says, which is exactly what you should report it as saying.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established government registry. Not fetched during this review; the FAA has changed registry inquiry URLs before, so confirm the current entry point.

tools.name: MarineTraffic
tools.summary: The largest AIS vessel-tracking platform, with live positions, port calls and vessel particulars.
tools.description:
MarineTraffic aggregates AIS broadcasts from a global network of coastal receivers plus satellite AIS, and presents live and historical vessel positions, port call records, vessel particulars and photographs.

Maritime investigation runs on AIS. Sanctions evasion, illegal fishing, arms shipments and smuggling all leave AIS traces, and the absences in those traces are frequently the story: vessels going dark near a sanctioned port, or transmitting a position that contradicts satellite imagery, or two vessels loitering together in a pattern consistent with a ship-to-ship transfer.

The critical technical fact, which distinguishes AIS from ADS-B, is that AIS position and identity are self-reported by the vessel and are straightforwardly spoofable. Vessels routinely broadcast false positions or another ship's identity. AIS data tells you what a transponder transmitted, not where a ship was. Corroborate with satellite imagery, port records or Equasis particulars before making any claim about a vessel's actual movements. Coastal receiver coverage is also good near shore and dependent on paid satellite AIS in open ocean, where much of the interesting behaviour occurs.
tools.costNotes: Free live map with delayed positions and limited history. Paid subscription tiers add real-time satellite AIS, extended history, port call records, fleet tracking and export, and a commercial API is sold separately. Current prices were not verified in this review.
tools.legalNotes: AIS is a mandatory unencrypted safety broadcast and receiving it is lawful. Terms of service restrict scraping and redistribution, and satellite AIS in particular is licensed data with real contractual constraints on republication. Crew members are identifiable in some associated records — vessel investigation can shade into surveillance of individual seafarers, which needs justification.
tools.reliabilityNotes: The platform faithfully reports received AIS, but AIS itself is self-reported and spoofing is common and well documented, including in sanctions-evasion cases where it is deliberate. Gaps have at least three innocent explanations — no receiver, equipment failure, legitimate safety-related silence — before you reach the interesting one. Rated 3 because the underlying signal is untrustworthy by nature, not because the platform is poor. Never assert a vessel's position from AIS alone.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established market-leading platform. Not fetched during this review; tier structure and pricing change periodically.

tools.name: VesselFinder
tools.summary: AIS vessel tracking with a usable free tier — the standard second source for corroborating a ship movement.
tools.description:
VesselFinder is an AIS aggregator in the same category as MarineTraffic, with live positions, vessel particulars, port calls and photographs, drawing on its own terrestrial receiver network and satellite AIS.

Its role in a rigorous workflow is corroboration. Because both platforms depend on the same underlying broadcasts but different receiver networks and different processing, comparing them tests whether a track is a genuine reception artefact or a data-handling difference. If a vessel appears in one and not the other over the same window, that discrepancy needs explaining before either is cited.

Its free tier is somewhat more usable than the leading competitor's for basic lookups, which makes it a practical default for quick checks. Everything in the MarineTraffic entry about AIS being self-reported and spoofable applies identically and is not repeated here because it is not a small caveat.
tools.costNotes: Free live map and basic vessel lookups. Paid tiers add satellite AIS, history, fleet monitoring and API access. Current prices were not verified in this review.
tools.legalNotes: As with MarineTraffic: receiving AIS is lawful, terms of service restrict scraping and redistribution, and satellite AIS is licensed data with republication constraints.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Reliable as a faithful presentation of received AIS, with the same fundamental limitation that AIS identity and position are self-reported and spoofable. Receiver coverage differs from MarineTraffic's, which is precisely why it is useful as a cross-check and why a difference between the two is informative rather than alarming.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established service. Not fetched during this review; pricing unverified.

tools.name: Equasis
tools.summary: Free public database of merchant ship particulars, ownership, management and inspection history.
tools.description:
Equasis is a public-interest maritime safety information system supported by a group of maritime administrations and the European Commission, with the IMO holding observer status. It publishes safety and ownership information on merchant ships, drawing on more than 50 contributing data providers and covering more than 85,000 ships — in practice, effectively every merchant vessel in service above 100 gross tonnage.

Its investigative value is ownership, and it is the free source that matters most in maritime work. Equasis distinguishes registered owner, ship manager, ISM manager and beneficial owner where reported, and gives each entity an IMO company number. That company number is a stable identifier you can search on to find every other vessel connected to the same operator — which is the mechanic by which sanctioned or high-risk fleets get mapped.

It also carries port state control inspection history and detentions, a good proxy for how a vessel is actually operated. Limits: it covers merchant shipping, so fishing vessels, yachts and naval ships are largely absent, and the ownership layers reported are frequently themselves shell companies requiring corporate research to penetrate.
tools.costNotes: Access is free of charge, but registration with a valid email address is required before the search functions can be used; the email address becomes your user identifier. Registration remained free as confirmed in early 2026.
tools.legalNotes: A public-interest system with terms directed at safety and transparency purposes; bulk extraction and commercial redistribution are not what it is provided for, and the terms of use should be read before any automated collection. Company and ownership records concern legal entities more than natural persons, which keeps data-protection exposure comparatively low.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Data comes from classification societies, port state control regimes and maritime administrations, which is high-quality provenance for this domain. Ownership fields are only as good as what was reported, and the deliberate use of layered shell ownership in shipping means the named owner is often a formality rather than a controller. Inspection history is authoritative. Some fields lag changes by months.
tools.confidenceNotes: Confirmed during this review: free access with mandatory free registration, coverage of more than 85,000 ships from more than 50 data providers, and IMO observer status.

tools.name: Global Fishing Watch
tools.summary: Open platform mapping industrial fishing and vessel activity from AIS and satellite data, with analysis-ready datasets.
tools.description:
Global Fishing Watch, a non-profit founded through a partnership involving Oceana, SkyTruth and Google, processes AIS and satellite data to identify and classify vessel behaviour at sea — distinguishing transit from apparent fishing activity, detecting encounters between vessels, and flagging loitering and AIS gaps.

That behavioural classification is what makes it different from a plain AIS tracker. Rather than a position history you get inferred activity, which is directly relevant to investigations of illegal fishing, forced labour at sea, sanctions evasion and transshipment. Its encounter and gap detection is particularly useful: an AIS gap followed by an encounter is the classic signature of a covert transfer.

The map is free and public, and datasets, code and APIs are published for research use. The essential caution is that the classifications are model outputs, not observations. 'Apparent fishing effort' is an inference from movement patterns and is explicitly labelled as apparent. Presenting a model's inference as an observed fact is the central failure mode with this tool, and the organisation's own documentation is careful about the distinction.
tools.costNotes: The map is free to use with no paywall. Datasets, code and APIs are published openly for research and public use, with API access requiring registration. Operates as a non-profit.
tools.legalNotes: Open data published for public-interest use, with dataset-specific terms and attribution requirements. Because outputs are inferences about the behaviour of identified vessels and by extension their operators, publishing an allegation of illegal activity based on a model output without corroboration carries real defamation risk.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Methodologically transparent, peer-reviewed in parts, and unusually honest about uncertainty — the term 'apparent fishing effort' is deliberate. Reliability of the underlying AIS is subject to the same spoofing and gap problems as any AIS source, and the classification models have real false-positive and false-negative rates. Excellent for identifying patterns worth investigating; not sufficient on its own to establish that a specific vessel did a specific illegal thing.
tools.confidenceNotes: Homepage fetched during this review: live, actively publishing as of August 2026, map free to use, with open datasets and APIs offered.
